newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ manufacturer confidence up depite lower profits.
newsitem.headline: NZ manufacturer confidence up depite lower profits.

text.p: Business confidence among New Zealand manufacturers is improving despite an expectation of profit declines, the Manufacturers' Federation said on Monday.

The WestpacTrust manufacturers business confidence survey, undertaken by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research for ManFed, also revealed New Zealand industry was moving into new management territory, ManFed said.

Confidence among South Island manufacturers, and exporters generally, recorded a dramatic lift. Confidence in the sector overall came out slightly on the positive side, with North Island manufacturers less pessimistic than they were about the
"But for the first time in years industry expects its profits to be in decline at a time when confidence is improving," ManFed said.
Profit levels had been falling across all regions and sizes of firms for the past two years, since the Reserve Bank tightened monetary supply in December 1994.
Profits for the March 1997 quarter are expected to be down even more than lately which has implications for government's projected surpluses, ManFed said.

"Not surprisingly, investment intentions are continuing to dwindle, except for South Island manufacturers which are up. Exporters and big firms by and large plan to keep their investment programmes ticking over."
ManFed said the good news for producer inflation was that despite the capacity utilisation index moving up slightly over the last quarter, there was plenty of spare capacity available.
"Small firms in particular indicate the contraint to their growth is a lack of affordable finance, not capacity."
ManFed said manufacturers across the board were taking "just-in-time" production methods across new thresholds.
"Industry has been slashing back its stock holdings of raw materials for the last four quarters and the intention is to cut back more yet -- this is unique to our experience.
"It means manufacturers are only buying components and other inputs once they are confident of firm orders for the finished goods to be made from them."
ManFed said that firms were also now happier than they were about their overall levels of finished goods held in stock, though they intended to reduce these holdings much more yet.
